title: The Moon’s Record Book
sub: Grades 3–4 · Our Incredible Moon · Craters, a giant crash and a piece of the Moon
objective: Students will learn that scientists think the Moon was born in a giant crash, and that its cratered face is a **record** of the space rocks that have struck it for billions of years. They will make craters in a model, find out why the Moon keeps its marks when Earth wears them away, and think about how scientists work out a story no one was there to see.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: No one was there to watch the Moon form, or to see most of its craters made. Scientists read the clues that are left, the way a detective reads a scene.

items.text: tell how scientists think the Moon was born: in a giant crash, about 4.5 billion years ago

items.text: explain why the Moon’s cratered face is a record of space rocks

materials: A deep tray or baking pan of flour, smoothed flat, with a thin dusting of cocoa powder on top
Pebbles or marbles of two sizes; a ruler; newspaper under the tray
Page 3 of this plan, projected or printed
connection: **On the poster** *Our Incredible Moon*, find the giant crash. **In the display case**, look for the lunar meteorite Adrar 013.

steps.title: A face full of marks
script: Show the Moon from the poster on the screen or page 3. Ask: *“What made all the round marks on the Moon’s face?”* Take every idea without judging: volcanoes, holes, rocks, aliens. Write a few on the board. *“Today you are Moon scientists. By the end, you will test one of these ideas yourselves.”*

screen.alt: The Moon rising on the poster: a huge lavender Moon, its face covered in gray patches and round marks
screen.caption: What made all the round marks on the Moon’s face?

steps.purpose: Wonder at the Moon’s marks before anyone names them.
students: What do you notice about the Moon’s face?
What could have made the round marks?

steps.title: A giant crash
script: **A giant crash.** Play the sound and read the poster: *“Scientists think an object about the size of Mars, nicknamed Theia, slammed into the young Earth about 4.5 billion years ago. The debris from that collision came together to form our Moon.”* No one saw it happen. *Probably* is an honest scientist’s word.

screen.question: Scientists think the Moon was born in a giant crash. Listen.

steps.purpose: Hear the poster’s first chapter: how the Moon was probably born.
students: What crashed into the young Earth?

steps.title: A record of space rocks
script: **A record.** Read: *“Additionally, the Moon’s cratered face is a record of the space rocks that have struck our corner of the solar system for billions of years.”* A record keeps a trace of what happened, like a diary. The display case holds a genuine **lunar meteorite**, Adrar 013: a rock from the Moon that reached Earth.

screen.text: Additionally, the Moon’s cratered face is a record of the space rocks that have struck our corner of the solar system for billions of years.

steps.purpose: Name the craters, and hear why the poster calls them a record.
students: What does the Moon’s face record?

steps.title: No wind, no rain
script: **No wind, no rain.** On Earth, wind and rain wear marks away. Read: *“The Moon has no wind or rain, so unless a meteorite happens to strike them, the astronauts’ footprints will probably last for millions of years.”* If footprints can last for millions of years, ask what that means for craters.

screen.text: The Moon has no wind or rain, so unless a meteorite happens to strike them, the astronauts’ footprints will probably last for millions of years.

steps.purpose: Understand why marks on the Moon last so long.
students: What wears marks away on Earth?
Why do marks on the Moon last?

steps.title: Drop, look, measure
script: Gather round the tray. A volunteer drops a pebble from 20 cm, measured with a ruler; another drops the same pebble from 60 cm, in a fresh spot. Measure each crater across. Look at the cocoa: the flour underneath is thrown out around the crater. Then gently blow across one crater, and sweep a finger over another. *“That is what wind and rain do on Earth. On the Moon, nothing smooths them away.”*

screen.question: Does a rock dropped from higher up make a bigger crater?

steps.purpose: Test an idea with a model, fairly: change one thing at a time.
students: Drop from 20 cm, then from 60 cm. Same pebble.
Measure each crater across. Look at the cocoa.

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students then choose a handout and record the lab. All three ask why the Moon keeps its record.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Number the Moon’s story in order. Draw the two craters and circle which is bigger. Finish sentences about wind and rain from a word bank.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Fill in the Moon’s story from a word bank. Record three drops in a table and state the pattern. Explain why Earth wipes its record clean and the Moon does not.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Read four overlapping craters and order them, oldest first. Plan and record a fair test. Explain how the model is like the Moon and how it is not.

steps.purpose: Record the lab and explain the Moon’s record, at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three record the crater lab.

steps.title: Look back
script: Ask the objectives back as questions, from the screen or page 1: *“Can you now…?”* For each one, students show a thumb up, sideways or down; for the last, ask a Red Level student to name what the flour model cannot show.

steps.title: How do we know?
script: End with the poster’s question: *“No one was there to watch the Moon form. How can scientists work out what probably happened billions of years ago?”* Craters, debris and Moon rocks are clues: evidence left behind.

screen.question: No one was there to watch the Moon form. How can scientists work out what probably happened billions of years ago?

steps.purpose: Close with the poster’s own question about evidence.
students: What clues are left for scientists to read?
